In [[mathematics]], the notion of a '''cliquish function''' is similar to, but weaker than, the notion of a [[continuous function]] and [[quasi-continuous function]]. All (quasi-)continuous functions are cliquish but the converse is not true in general.

==Definition==

Let <math> X </math> be a [[topological space]].  A real-valued function <math> f:X \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> is cliquish at a point <math> x \in X </math> if for any <math> \epsilon > 0 </math> and any [[open neighborhood]] <math> U </math> of <math> x </math> there is a non-empty [[open set]] <math> G \subset U </math> such that

<math display="block">  |f(y) - f(z)| < \epsilon \;\;\;\; \forall y,z \in G </math>

Note that in the above definition, it is not necessary that <math> x \in G </math>.

==Properties==

* If <math> f: X \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> is (quasi-)continuous then <math> f</math> is cliquish.
* If <math> f: X \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> and <math> g: X \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> are quasi-continuous, then <math> f+g </math> is cliquish.
* If <math> f: X \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> is cliquish then <math> f</math> is the sum of two quasi-continuous functions.

==Example==

Consider the function <math> f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> defined by <math> f(x) = 0 </math> whenever <math> x \leq 0 </math> and <math> f(x) = 1 </math> whenever <math> x > 0 </math>.  Clearly f is continuous everywhere except at x=0, thus cliquish everywhere except (at most) at x=0.  At x=0, take any open neighborhood U of x.  Then there exists an open set <math> G \subset U </math> such that <math> y,z < 0 \; \forall y,z \in G </math>.  Clearly this yields  <math> |f(y) - f(z)| = 0  \; \forall y \in G</math> thus f is cliquish.

In contrast, the function  <math> g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> defined by <math> g(x) = 0 </math> whenever <math> x</math> is a rational number and <math> g(x) = 1 </math> whenever <math> x</math> is an irrational number is nowhere cliquish, since every nonempty open set <math>G</math> contains some <math>y_1, y_2</math> with <math>|g(y_1) - g(y_2)| = 1</math>.
